prime.problem: "Decode is memory-bound" means nothing until you know what the memory is, how far it sits from the math units, and how much math those units can do. Without a picture of the chip, every later optimisation (tiling, batching, fusing, quantizing) looks like an unrelated trick.
prime.fits: First card of the machine half. The FLOPs card counted the work; this card describes the H100 that does it. The roofline card next combines its two headline numbers (989 TF/s and 3.35 TB/s) into one ratio.
prime.goal: Sketch an H100 from memory with its sizes and bandwidths, and explain why a batch-1 decode step leaves the tensor cores idle about 99.7% of the time.

attend: Why can't Llama-3.1-8B's weights stay on chip between decode steps, even with a 50 MB L2?
What happens inside a warp when its threads take different sides of an if/else?
Tensor cores give 15× the CUDA cores' FLOPs. Which parts of a transformer can't use them?
Why does an H200 decode faster than an H100 when both have the same compute?
How does an SM keep its math units busy while a memory read is still in flight?

must: Each memory level is smaller and closer to the math (80 GB HBM → 50 MB L2 → 256 KB SMEM per SM → registers) → 16.06 GB of weights is 321× the L2 → the weights can't stay on chip → every decode step streams them from HBM: ≈ 4.8 ms at 3.35 TB/s
Tensor cores do matrix multiply-accumulate → 990 vs 66 TF/s on the CUDA cores (15×) → matmul-shaped work in a supported precision runs fast → softmax, norms and activations don't get that speed
Batch-1 decode needs 16.2 µs of math but 4.8 ms of reads → the tensor cores sit idle ≈ 99.7% of the step → for decode speed buy bandwidth (an H200 over an H100), not FLOPs

An SM keeps up to 64 warps resident → when one waits on memory, another runs → latency is hidden by switching, not by caching everything → but only if each thread uses few enough registers to leave room for many warps
elevated: A warp's 32 threads run one instruction together (SIMT) → an if/else split runs both branches in turn with the idle lanes masked → divergent code wastes lanes
Registers are 64 KB per sub-partition → at 256 registers per thread only 8 warps fit per SM instead of 64 → fewer warps to switch between, less latency hiding
reference: NVLink 450 GB/s per H100, 900 on B200
V100/A100 SMEM sizes and tensor-core FLOPs per cycle
TPU VMEM of about 128 MB on v5p

compress.prompt: Draw the H100 from memory as nested boxes (chip → SM → sub-partition) with the four memory levels, each labelled with its size and, where published, its bandwidth. Then write one sentence on which arrow a decode step spends its time waiting on.
checklist: 132 SMs, each with 4 sub-partitions holding a tensor core, 32 CUDA cores and 64 KB of registers
SMEM/L1 256 KB per SM, L2 50 MB shared, HBM 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s
tensor cores 990 TF/s vs CUDA cores 66 TF/s
the weights are 321× the L2, so they're streamed from HBM every step
decode waits on the HBM arrow, so the tensor cores are idle about 99.7% of the time

retrieve.q: Explain why a GPU keeps thousands of threads resident instead of running a few very fast ones like a CPU.
answer: a read from HBM takes a long time
with many resident warps the SM switches to one that is ready and hides the wait
a CPU's few big cores (8 on the M3) suit branchy sequential work but have too few lanes and too little bandwidth to stream 16 GB per token

retrieve.q: Follow one weight from HBM to a tensor core during a matmul: which levels does it pass through, and who manages each one?
answer: HBM: you allocate it (global memory, cudaMalloc)
L2: hardware only; you can only shape access patterns
SMEM: you as shared memory (tiles for the tensor cores), or hardware as L1
registers: the compiler, then the tensor core's multiply-accumulate

retrieve.q: Using the card's register numbers, how many warps can one SM keep resident if every thread uses 256 registers, and why should a kernel writer care?
answer: 4 sub-partitions × 16,384 registers = 65,536 per SM
256 × 32 threads = 8,192 registers per warp → 8 warps, instead of the maximum 64
fewer resident warps means fewer to switch to while one waits on memory

retrieve.q: Pick a chip to maximise single-user tokens/s on Llama-3.1-8B in BF16: an H100, an H200, or a hypothetical chip with 2× the H100's FLOPs and the same bandwidth. Rank them and justify it.
answer: H200 first: 4.8 TB/s → about 3.35 ms per step, ≈ 299 tok/s ceiling (computed)
the H100 and the 2×-FLOPs chip tie at 3.35 TB/s → ≈ 209 tok/s
extra FLOPs don't help batch-1 decode; they would help prefill

compare.q: Your M3 vs an H100 as machines for the same job: what is fundamentally different, which hardware choice causes most of the decode gap, when is the M3 the right tool, and how does each fall short?
answer: the M3 shares one 24 GB pool between CPU and GPU at ~100 GB/s; the H100 has 80 GB of HBM at 3.35 TB/s
bandwidth causes the 33.5× gap in decode ceilings (6.2 vs 209 tok/s for 8B BF16)
the M3 fits one user running a small quantized model
the M3 falls short on bandwidth and memory for big models or many users; the H100 wastes its FLOPs at batch 1

compare.q: This card gives the chip's two headline numbers; the roofline card turns them into one ratio. What does that ratio capture, and what from this card does it hide?
answer: C ÷ W = 295: FLOPs the chip can do per byte it moves
it hides that non-matmul work runs on CUDA cores (a ridge near 20, not 295)
it hides caches: data kept in L2 or SMEM doesn't cost HBM bandwidth
it hides launch and scheduling overhead on tiny operations

predict.q: A B200 has 148 SMs, a 126 MB L2 and 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. Before computing: could Llama-3.1-8B's BF16 weights live in its L2, and what batch-1 decode ceiling do you expect?
predict.answer: No: 16.06 GB is about 127× the 126 MB L2, so the weights are still streamed from HBM every step. The ceiling scales with bandwidth: 8e12 ÷ 16.06e9 ≈ 498 tok/s, the same figure the serving-metrics card gives.

apply.task: Build a one-page machine sheet for Llama-3.1-8B BF16 on five chips: H100, H200, B200, TPU v5e and your M3. For each give ops:byte (C ÷ W), whether 16.06 GB fits, the batch-1 decode ceiling (W ÷ 16.06 GB) and the 1,000-token prefill floor (2 × 8.03e9 × 1,000 ÷ C) where C is known.
apply.done: H100: 295, fits, 209 tok/s, 16.2 ms. H200: 206, fits, ≈ 299 tok/s, 16.2 ms. B200: 281, fits, ≈ 498 tok/s, 7.1 ms. TPU v5e: 240, doesn't fit in 16 GB. M3: ops:byte unknown, fits in 24 GB, 6.2 tok/s, prefill floor unknown (all computed from the course's specs).
apply.hint: H200: 989 TF/s and 4.8 TB/s. B200: 2,250 TF/s and 8 TB/s. Only the decode column needs bandwidth alone.
